title: Performance: Optimizing existing content
description: This post is about optimizing existing content for better performance. As an example, I’ll use the Demo UI for LogiFront 2.0, available at demo.logifront.com. Note: The demo is not a working app
body_html:
This post is about optimizing existing content for better performance.
As an example, I’ll use the Demo UI for LogiFront 2.0, available at demo.logifront.com.

Note: The demo is not a working app, just HTML and CSS for demo-purposes.

The initial size of the index.html-file is 175kb. This isn’t so bad, since the file contains the html for all the various dialogs and templates that is used in the complete app — but we can do better!

Minifying

First, I minified the html using HTML Minifier.
This reduced the size to 70kb!

In the regular, un-minified version of index.html, the amount of DOM-nodes is 4254.

Now, let’s count*) the amount of DOM-nodes in the minified version:
2463!
That’s 1791 less DOM-nodes to parse.
Why is that?
Because all line-breaks create empty text-nodes, and because HTML Minifier removes comment-tags.

Gzipping

Gzip is the web-equivalent of zip, rar or stuffIt. It can either be dynamic (see your web-server documentation) or static/manual.
In this example, since the html for the main app won’t change that much, let’s use static/manual gzip, so the server won’t waste processing time gzipping the file, every time a user request it.

I used 7-Zip to gzip the file (now index.html.gz) to 9.8kb!
That’s less than 6% of the original file-size.

Content Headers

A web-server or Content Delivery Network (CDN) won’t know that the gzipped file is actually a html-file. I use Amazon S3 CDN;
Here’s how to “tell” S3 what the file is:

1. Rename the file from “index.html.gz” to “index.html”.
2. Change the Content-Type-header, and add a Content-Encoding-header:

Content-Type : text/html
Content-Encoding: gzip

The “Content-Type” tells the browser it’s an html-file, although it’s actually a gzip-file.
The “Content-Encoding” tells the browser that the file is encoded with gzip.

We can also tell S3 to use Cache-Control by adding this header:

Cache-Control: max-age=31536000

Other types

This method can also be used for other file-types: CSS, JavaScript, SVG, Fonts etc., with small modifications:

CSS
Content-Type : text/css
JavaScript
Content-Type : application/x-javascript
EOT, TTF & WOFF
Content-Type : application/octet-stream
SVG
Content-Type : image/svg+xml

Is you’re using a CSS-pre-processor like SASS or LESS, set it to output the CSS as Compressed.
Otherwise, use a dedicated minifier like cssminifier.com.

For JavaScript, I use Google Closure (Advanced) — but most pre-processors have a minifier-option for JavaScript as well.

Result

So, without changing a single line of code, we ended up with this:
1. HTML went from 175kb to 9.8kb.
2. CSS-files went from 67kb (combined) to 14.7kb (combined).
3. Font-files went from 105kb (combined) to 40kb (combined).

The total amount of kilobytes went from 347kb to 64.5kb = 18.62% of the original size, more than 5 times faster to download — and with 1791 fewer nodes to parse.

Who should do this?

So — who should complete these performance-tasks? It doesn’t have to be a front- or backend-developer, since these changes don’t require any programming skills. Maybe, as Ilya Grigorik suggests in his new book, High Performance Browser Networking, it’s time to add a new member to the web-team:
The performance engineer.

A performance engineer could/should:

  1. Work closely with both front- and backend-developers, analyzing load-times, reviewing load-waterfalls, reviewing a site with both ySlow and Page Speed.
  2. Optimize the web-server: remove unnecessary headers, setting up cache-control, content-headers, gzip etc.
  3. Optimize network-performance — start by reading High Performance Browser Networking.

*) I used a snippet for counting the DOM-nodes.
If you haven’t used snippets before, read this article.

Node.prototype.countChildNodes = function() {
  return this.hasChildNodes()
    ? Array.prototype.slice.apply(this.childNodes).map(function(el) {
        return 1 + el.countChildNodes();
      }).reduce(function(previousValue, currentValue, index, array){
        return previousValue + currentValue;
      })
    : 0;
};
document.countChildNodes();

Run the snippet with CTRL+ENTER.
